title: How contract law fits together
summary: Contract law determines which commitments create legal duties, what those duties require, and what relief follows when they are broken. The governing source of law must be identified before applying a formation checklist.
notes:
Begin with the transaction. The common law consists of rules developed through judicial decisions; the relevant jurisdiction’s cases matter. The Restatement collects and organizes general common-law principles. It is persuasive authority rather than an enacted statute. The Uniform Commercial Code is a model whose enacted state version supplies statutory rules. Article 2 principally governs transactions in goods, while Article 1 supplies shared definitions and background rules. Under § 1-103(b), principles of law and equity supplement the Code unless a particular Code provision displaces them.

The United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, abbreviated CISG, is a treaty governing qualifying international sales. It has its own rules of formation, interpretation, and remedies. It is not simply another name for Article 2 or for the Restatement. The assigned TeeVee Toons excerpt illustrates why a court may consider negotiations and intent under CISG Articles 8 and 11 even though a domestic parol-evidence approach might treat a writing differently. The precise scope, exclusions, declarations, and any effective choice require checking the applicable text; the separately assigned Selections volume is not fully available here.

Once the governing law is identified, ask what was communicated and agreed; what supports legal enforcement; whether sufficient certainty and required form exist; and whether a defense limits enforcement. After that, identify the terms, conditions, performance, any excuse, and the remedy. These questions interact: interpretation can establish an implied promise, and a statutory form requirement can prevent enforcement even where an agreement exists. The sequence is a study framework synthesized from the cited readings, not a single rule announced by one court.

topics.governing-law: The source of law determines which formation and enforcement rules apply.

route.title: 1. Identify the governing law
route.text: Determine which jurisdiction and body of law govern the transaction. Article 2 supplies special rules for sales of goods. A qualifying international sale may instead fall under the CISG. Common-law rules and statutory rules must be read together, with attention to what the statute replaces.

route.title: 2. Identify the commitment and the agreement
route.text: Ask what the parties communicated through their words and conduct, and what a reasonable recipient would understand in that setting. Offer and acceptance are common ways of showing agreement. Agreement to a transaction and agreement to a particular term can present different questions.

route.title: 3. Identify the basis for enforcement
route.text: In the ordinary bargain, each side gives or promises something sought in exchange for the other side’s undertaking. Reliance can support enforcement in circumstances addressed by promissory estoppel. A benefit conferred can also raise a separate restitution claim, even when no promise is enforceable.

route.title: 4. Check certainty and required form
route.text: Determine whether the obligation is sufficiently definite and whether an applicable statute requires a signed writing or other evidence. An agreement may exist while a form requirement prevents its enforcement. Separate doctrines and statutory exceptions may change that result.

route.title: 5. Check defects in the bargain and limits on enforcement
route.text: Examine the circumstances that produced agreement, including threats, deception, and the opportunity to understand the terms. Unconscionability and public policy can limit enforcement even when the ordinary formation requirements have been satisfied.

route.title: 6. Determine the actual obligations
route.text: Interpret the language, decide what evidence may be considered, and determine whether the writing contains the whole agreement. Trade usage, prior dealings, statutory terms, and duties of good faith may affect the obligations. A contract can give a party discretion while limiting how it exercises that discretion.

route.title: 7. Determine when performance is due and whether it was supplied
route.text: Distinguish a promise from a condition that must occur before performance is due. Consider the order of the exchange, the significance of defects, and any waiver or prevention of a condition. A failure can justify damages without necessarily justifying termination of the entire relationship.

route.title: 8. Examine allocated risks and possible excuses
route.text: Ask whether a mistake or a later event affects a basic assumption, who bears the relevant risk, and whether the governing doctrine excuses performance. The contract’s own allocation of risk matters before a court supplies an excuse.

route.title: 9. Identify the claimant and the appropriate relief
route.text: Determine who can enforce the obligation, including an intended beneficiary or an assignee. Then identify the protected interest and remedy. Expectation, reliance, restitution, specific relief, and agreed damages operate with different requirements and limits.
